title: Cabinet Clears Rs 14,500 Crore Storage Fund Backing 92 GWh of New Grid Capacity
excerpt: The viability gap funding scheme covers 60 GWh of pumped hydro, 30 GWh of battery storage and 2 GWh of alternative technologies through 2030-31, against an estimated total investment of Rs 97,600 crore.
body:
• The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a Rs 14,500 crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity that is yet to be commissioned, running from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.
  • The capacity is split 60 GWh pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 2 GWh of alternative storage technologies, with total estimated investment of Rs 97,600 crore.
  • The new capacity equals about 170 per cent of India present grid-scale storage, against an estimated requirement of 411 GWh by 2031-32 — so the scheme covers roughly a fifth of the assessed need.
  • Battery projects under the scheme must meet a minimum 40 per cent domestic content requirement; public and private distribution companies are eligible for support for battery and pumped hydro projects.

India has put a price on closing its grid storage gap. The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a viability gap funding scheme of Rs 14,500 crore for the development of grid-scale energy storage systems over FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, according to the official statement reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. VGF is a capital grant: the government covers part of a project cost so the project can price its service at a level buyers will accept, and the rest of the money here — the scheme expects total investment of about Rs 97,600 crore — must come from project developers and lenders.

Where the 92 GWh goes

The largest share is not batteries. Of the 92 GWh, 60 GWh is hydro pumped storage, 30 GWh is battery energy storage systems and 2 GWh is alternative or emerging storage technologies, according to Upstox News, summarising the official statement. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for the funding for battery and pumped hydro projects. To push domestic manufacturing, battery projects carry a minimum domestic content requirement of 40 per cent.

The gap this is meant to close

The statement frames the scheme against a requirement of 411 GWh of grid-scale storage by 2031-32. The 92 GWh supported here equals about 170 per cent of the country present grid-scale storage capacity — a measure of how small the installed base still is. Solar and wind generation is cheapest when the sun shines and the wind blows; storage is what lets a grid use that power in the evening peak. Without it, renewable capacity additions translate into curtailment rather than supply.

At the same Cabinet meeting, the government also approved a separate Rs 2,814 crore scheme to support processing of critical minerals including lithium and nickel inside the country over the same five-year period — the upstream half of the same strategy, since battery storage built with 40 per cent domestic content still needs processed minerals.

What to watch next

Wednesday decision is an approval, not a tender. The release does not set dates for the first bids or say how the 92 GWh will be shared among states. The scheme guidelines, the per-project grant caps and the first auction calendar from the Ministry of Power are the documents that will turn the Rs 14,500 crore headline into bankable projects, and they are the next things investors and developers should look for.
